title: Server-Side Visualization Tools in Python
text:
Where does a visualization run?


Static graphic: rendered once; export a PNG, SVG, or PDF (Matplotlib, Seaborn, ggplot2).
Client-side interactive graphic: browser handles zoom, hover, and selection (Plotly.js, Vega-Lite).
Server-backed data app: browser controls trigger Python/R calculations, queries, or models (Streamlit, Dash, Shiny).
These categories overlap: a Streamlit app can display an interactive Plotly chart.

title: Server-Side Visualization Tools in Python
text:
The internet in one picture


A browser (client) requests a page from a web server.
The server returns HTML, CSS, JavaScript, and possibly data.
The browser displays the page; later interactions may or may not require another server request.
Historical diagram note: Java applets are obsolete; modern web apps generally use JavaScript and web APIs.

title: Server-Side Visualization Tools in Python
text:
Frontend vs. backend


Frontend (browser): what users see and click; HTML/CSS/JavaScript.
Backend (server): Python/R code that loads data, runs models, queries databases, and returns results.
A server can be your own laptop during development—not necessarily a cloud machine.
Streamlit hides much of the web plumbing, but a server process still runs Python.

title: Server-Side Visualization Tools in Python
text:
A concrete example: exploring sales
Client-side-only: A user hovers over a precomputed sales chart or hides a product series.
Server-backed: A user chooses a region → Python filters millions of records (or queries a database) → computes a new forecast → sends updated results to the browser.

A backend unlocks fresh data, expensive computation, authentication, and coordinated controls.
Tradeoff: hosting, latency, cost, and security become important.

The UI collects inputs and presents outputs.
The server does work that cannot be packaged as a self-contained HTML chart.
A browser is still responsible for rendering the final visualization.

Hosting: where does the backend live?

Local: run on your laptop for development; browser connects to localhost.
Hosted: deploy to an appropriate cloud/app platform so others can open a URL.
Hosting must keep the Python/R process running and provide required packages and data access.
Public hosting is not automatically private: avoid committing passwords, tokens, or sensitive datasets.
Containerization (e.g., Docker) can help package dependencies, but is not needed for our first app.

title: Server-Side Visualization Tools in Python
text:
What is Streamlit?

Streamlit is an open-source Python framework for making interactive data applications.
Write ordinary Python scripts with functions such as st.title(), st.slider(), and st.plotly_chart().
Streamlit supplies the browser interface and runs your Python code on a server.
Great for prototypes, course projects, exploratory dashboards, and model demos.

Mental model: write a Python script that describes the page.

title: Server-Side Visualization Tools in Python
text:
Install and launch
From a terminal in your project directory:
python -m pip install streamlit pandas plotly
Create a file called app.py. Run:
streamlit run app.py

Open the local URL printed in the terminal (typically http://localhost:8501).
Save edits to app.py; Streamlit can rerun the app.
Important: Run a Streamlit app from a terminal—not as a normal Jupyter code cell.

title: Server-Side Visualization Tools in Python
section: First app: text and a table
text:
First app: text and a table
Save this as app.py:
import streamlit as st
import pandas as pd

st.title("My first data app")
st.write("Explore a tiny dataset with Python.")

data = pd.DataFrame({"month": ["Jan", "Feb", "Mar"],
                     "sales": [120, 150, 135]})
st.dataframe(data)

st.title() creates a heading.
st.write() displays text or many Python objects.
st.dataframe() provides a scrollable, interactive table.

Add a widget: the slider
import streamlit as st

st.title("Interactive input")
minimum_sales = st.slider("Minimum sales", 0, 200, 100)
st.write("Selected threshold:", minimum_sales)

st.slider() returns the user’s chosen value.
Changing a widget typically reruns the Python script from top to bottom.
The widget’s current value is available on each rerun.

section: Connect an input to a visualization
text:
Connect an input to a visualization
import pandas as pd
import plotly.express as px
import streamlit as st

sales = pd.DataFrame({
    "month": ["Jan", "Feb", "Mar", "Apr"],
    "sales": [120, 150, 135, 180],
})
threshold = st.slider("Minimum sales", 0, 200, 100)
filtered = sales[sales["sales"] >= threshold]

fig = px.bar(filtered, x="month", y="sales", title="Monthly sales")
st.plotly_chart(fig, use_container_width=True)
Notice: Python filters the data; Plotly handles chart interactions in the browser.

title: Server-Side Visualization Tools in Python
text:
A complete small dashboard
import pandas as pd
import plotly.express as px
import streamlit as st

st.title("Sales explorer")
df = pd.DataFrame({"region": ["East", "East", "West", "West"],
                   "month": ["Jan", "Feb", "Jan", "Feb"],
                   "sales": [120, 160, 90, 140]})
region = st.selectbox("Region", sorted(df["region"].unique()))
view = df[df["region"] == region]
st.metric("Total sales", f"${view['sales'].sum():,.0f}")
st.plotly_chart(px.bar(view, x="month", y="sales"),
                use_container_width=True)
st.dataframe(view)

One selection drives a metric, chart, and table.
This is a server-backed dashboard, even though its dataset is small.

import streamlit as st

st.set_page_config(page_title="Explorer", layout="wide")
st.title("Explorer")

with st.sidebar:
    year = st.selectbox("Year", [2024, 2025, 2026])

left, right = st.columns(2)
with left:
    st.metric("Selected year", year)
with right:

Sidebar: controls that affect the whole page.
Columns: place related outputs side by side.
st.set_page_config() belongs near the beginning of the script.

import pandas as pd

uploaded = st.file_uploader("Choose a CSV", type="csv")

Validate file types, column names, and missing values before plotting.
Do not assume that a shared app’s uploads are appropriate for sensitive data.

Streamlit’s rerun model

The script normally runs top to bottom when a user changes a widget.
Widget values are re-created from the current browser session.
This makes small apps simple, but repeated data loading can be slow.
Ask: Which operations should happen on every interaction?

title: Server-Side Visualization Tools in Python
text:
Cache expensive work
import pandas as pd
import streamlit as st

@st.cache_data
def load_data(path):
    return pd.read_csv(path)

df = load_data("sales.csv")
st.dataframe(df.head())

st.cache_data is for reusable data results; cache entries can be shared across sessions.
Use st.cache_resource for reusable resources such as model objects or connections.
Choose caching carefully when data changes or contains user-specific information.

title: Server-Side Visualization Tools in Python
text:
Remember values across reruns
import streamlit as st

if "clicks" not in st.session_state:
    st.session_state.clicks = 0

if st.button("Count a click"):
    st.session_state.clicks += 1

st.write("Clicks in this session:", st.session_state.clicks)

st.session_state retains values for a user session across reruns.
Forms, tabs, multipage navigation, and callbacks offer additional control.

title: Server-Side Visualization Tools in Python
text:
Deployment and reproducibility

Keep app.py and a dependency file (such as requirements.txt) together.
Test locally from a clean environment before publishing.
Use a Streamlit-compatible hosting service or your own server/container.
Store secrets using platform-supported secret management—not in Git.
Check server logs, package versions, data access, and user permissions.

title: Server-Side Visualization Tools in Python
text:
Where Dash fits

Dash is a Python framework from Plotly for interactive web applications.
Uses explicit layout components and callbacks to connect inputs to outputs.
Often useful when you want more precise control over how UI events update specific outputs.
Streamlit usually offers a shorter path to a first analytical dashboard.
Both require a running Python app server for server-side functionality.

title: Server-Side Visualization Tools in Python
text:
Minimal Dash example
Install: python -m pip install dash plotly
from dash import Dash, dcc, html, Input, Output
import plotly.express as px

app = Dash(__name__)
app.layout = html.Div([
    dcc.Slider(1, 5, 1, id="minimum"),
    dcc.Graph(id="chart"),
])

@app.callback(Output("chart", "figure"), Input("minimum", "value"))
def update_chart(minimum):
    df = px.data.iris()
    return px.scatter(df[df.sepal_length >= minimum],
                      x="sepal_width", y="sepal_length",
                      color="species")

if __name__ == "__main__":
    app.run(debug=True)
Run: python app.py. The callback connects slider changes to the figure.

text:
Today’s roadmap

Getting started with Shiny: what it is, how an app is built, how to run it
What is a dashboard? and why some dashboards need a server
Dashboards with bslib: modern layouts with very little code
Demo: a fuel economy dashboard, then sharing it with the world

Everything is in the lecture folder:
shiny-lecture/
├── shiny-lecture.ipynb        <- these notes
├── apps/
│   ├── 01-hello-shiny/        <- first app
│   ├── 02-mpg-explorer/       <- more widgets, more reactivity
│   ├── 03-hello-bslib/        <- first dashboard
│   └── 04-mpg-dashboard/      <- final product
└── images/
Download the example apps
Here are nine slides for the front of the lecture. Each cell starts with a ## header, so you can split them into separate notebook cells where you like.
One small terminology point: when you run an app locally, Shiny starts a real web server, a small program running on your own computer, rather than a “virtual” one. The slides call it a “local server,” which keeps the idea you wanted.
# How the Web Works: Clients and Servers

The big picture behind every web app

## Clients and servers

Every time you use the web, two sides are talking:

- **Client:** the program that *asks* for something (usually your web browser)
- **Server:** the program that *answers* (sends back a page, data, or a result)

**Restaurant analogy**

| Restaurant | Web |
|---|---|
| Customer places an order | Browser sends a **request** |
| Kitchen prepares the food | Server does the work |
| Waiter brings the plate | Server sends a **response** |

- You never see the kitchen, only the plate
- Each click, search, or slider move can be a new request

## A server is a program, not just a machine

- "Server" often means a big computer in a data center, but strictly it is **software that listens for requests and answers them**
- Any computer can run a server, **including your laptop**
- One computer can run many servers at once

**Examples**

- Google's servers answer searches
- Canvas's servers send your grades and assignments
- Your laptop running a Shiny app: also a server

## Client-side vs. server-side tools

**Where does the work happen?**

| | Client-side | Server-side |
|---|---|---|
| Runs on | The viewer's browser | A server somewhere else |
| Examples | Plotly charts, Quarto websites, JavaScript | Shiny, Google search, online banking |
| Data | Sent to the browser in full | Stays on the server |
| Needs a running server? | No, just files to download | Yes, always on |
| Good for | Static sites, light interactivity | Live data, big data, computation, privacy |

- **Client-side:** the server hands over the files once, then your browser does everything
- **Server-side:** the browser keeps asking the server to do new work

## IP addresses: how computers find each other

- Every device on a network has an **IP address**, like a mailing address for computers
- Example: `142.250.80.46` (one of Google's servers)
- Names like `google.com` are translated into IP addresses for you, like looking up a phone number in a contact list

**Two special kinds**

- **Public IP:** reachable from the internet (a website's server)
- **Private IP:** only reachable inside your home or campus network (for example `192.168.1.25`)

## Ports: which program on the computer?

- One computer can run many servers at once, so an IP address alone is not enough
- A **port** is a numbered door on that computer, and each server listens at its own door

**Analogy:** the IP address is the apartment building, the port is the apartment number

| Port | Typical use |
|---|---|
| 80 | Regular websites (`http`) |
| 443 | Secure websites (`https`) |
| 8080, 3838, random numbers | Development servers, like a local Shiny app |

A full address looks like this: `http://142.250.80.46:443`

## localhost: your computer talking to itself

- **`localhost`** is a special name that always means **"this computer"**
- Its IP address is always **`127.0.0.1`**
- Requests to localhost never leave your machine; there is no internet involved
- Other people **cannot** open your localhost address, because on their computer it points to *their* machine

> `localhost` is like writing "me" as the address on a letter: it always comes back to you.

## Running a Shiny app locally

When you click **Run App**, R does three things:

1. Starts a small **web server** inside your R session
2. Picks a **port** and listens on `127.0.0.1`
3. Opens your browser (the **client**) at that address

```
Listening on http://127.0.0.1:4321
```

| Piece | Who plays it |
|---|---|
| Client | Your web browser |
| Server | Your R session |
| Address | `127.0.0.1` (localhost) |
| Port | `4321` (changes each run unless you choose one) |

- Client and server are on the **same computer**, but they still talk over the web, exactly like a real website
- This is why your R console is busy: it is serving the app

## Local vs. deployed

**Local (today)**

- The server is your laptop, at `127.0.0.1`
- Only you can open the app
- It stops when you close R or your laptop

**Deployed (end of lecture)**

- The server is an always-on computer with a public address
- Anyone with the link can open the app, for example `https://your-name.shinyapps.io/my-app/`
- Same app code, it just lives on a different server

> Deploying = moving the server from your laptop to a computer the whole internet can reach.
The “Local vs. deployed” slide sets up the deployment section at the end, so you can point back to it there.

text:
Anatomy of a Shiny app
Every app has exactly two parts plus one line that connects them.










UI (user interface): layout, inputs, and empty placeholders for outputs
Server: a function that turns inputs into outputs
shinyApp(ui, server): launches the app

title: Interactive Apps and Dashboards with Shiny
text:
Your first app
Create a folder 01-hello-shiny/ with one file named exactly app.R:
# ------------------------------------------------------------
# App 1: Hello, Shiny!
# The smallest useful Shiny app: two inputs, two outputs.
#
# Run it:
#   RStudio:       open this file and click "Run App"
#   R console:     shiny::runApp("01-hello-shiny")
#   Command line:  Rscript -e 'shiny::runApp("01-hello-shiny", launch.browser = TRUE)'
# ------------------------------------------------------------

library(shiny)

# ---- UI: what the user sees ---------------------------------
ui <- fluidPage(
  titlePanel("Hello, Shiny!"),

  sidebarLayout(
    sidebarPanel(
      textInput("name", "What is your name?", value = "student"),
      sliderInput("n", "Number of random points:",
                  min = 10, max = 1000, value = 100)
    ),

    mainPanel(
      textOutput("greeting"),
      plotOutput("hist")
    )
  )
)

# ---- Server: the logic behind the page ----------------------
server <- function(input, output, session) {

  # Re-runs whenever input$name changes
  output$greeting <- renderText({
    paste0("Hello, ", input$name, "! Here are ", input$n, " random numbers.")
  })

  # Re-runs whenever input$n changes
  output$hist <- renderPlot({
    hist(rnorm(input$n),
         col = "steelblue", border = "white",
         main = "Histogram of random values", xlab = "Value")
  })
}

# ---- Connect the two ----------------------------------------
shinyApp(ui = ui, server = server)

text:
The most common beginner bugs

Mismatched ids: plotOutput("histogram") but output$hist. Nothing appears, and there is no error.
Missing commas in the UI: the UI is one big nested function call, so elements are separated by commas
Forgetting the render function: output$hist <- hist(...) fails; it must be renderPlot({ hist(...) })
Reading inputs outside a reactive context: input$n only works inside render*(), reactive(), or observe*()
Wrong working directory: read.csv("data.csv") fails because the file is not inside the app folder

Debugging tip: add print(input$n) inside a render function and watch the console.

title: Interactive Apps and Dashboards with Shiny
text:
reactive(): compute once, use everywhere
Problem: several outputs need the same filtered data.
# Without reactive(): the filter runs 3 times
output$plot  <- renderPlot({ data <- filter(mpg, class == input$class); ... })
output$table <- renderTable({ data <- filter(mpg, class == input$class); ... })
output$count <- renderText({ data <- filter(mpg, class == input$class); ... })
# With reactive(): write it once, reuse it
filtered <- reactive({
  filter(mpg, class == input$class)
})

output$plot  <- renderPlot({ ggplot(filtered(), ...) })
output$table <- renderTable({ filtered() })
output$count <- renderText({ nrow(filtered()) })

Call it with parentheses: filtered()
Re-runs only when input$class changes, and caches the result
Less repeated code, faster apps

title: Interactive Apps and Dashboards with Shiny
text:
App 2: full code
# ------------------------------------------------------------
# App 2: MPG Explorer
# A classic Shiny app (not a dashboard) that shows off more widgets
# and the key reactivity tools:
#   - several input types (select, checkbox group, slider, radio)
#   - reactive() to share one filtered dataset across outputs
#   - tabsetPanel() for multiple views
#   - observeEvent() + update*Input() for a "Reset" button
#   - downloadHandler() to export the filtered data
#
# Run it:  shiny::runApp("02-mpg-explorer")
# ------------------------------------------------------------

library(shiny)
library(ggplot2)
library(dplyr)

# mpg ships with ggplot2: 234 cars from 1999 and 2008
cars <- mpg

# Friendly labels for the numeric variables users can plot
num_vars <- c(
  "Engine size (L)" = "displ",
  "City MPG"        = "cty",
  "Highway MPG"     = "hwy",
  "Cylinders"       = "cyl"
)

# ---- UI ------------------------------------------------------
ui <- fluidPage(
  titlePanel("MPG Explorer"),

  sidebarLayout(
    sidebarPanel(
      h4("Filter the cars"),

      selectInput("class", "Vehicle class:",
                  choices  = sort(unique(cars$class)),
                  selected = sort(unique(cars$class)),
                  multiple = TRUE),

      checkboxGroupInput("year", "Model year:",
                         choices  = c(1999, 2008),
                         selected = c(1999, 2008),
                         inline   = TRUE),

      sliderInput("displ", "Engine size (L):",
                  min = min(cars$displ), max = max(cars$displ),
                  value = range(cars$displ), step = 0.1),

      hr(),
      h4("Plot settings"),

      selectInput("x", "X axis:", choices = num_vars, selected = "displ"),
      selectInput("y", "Y axis:", choices = num_vars, selected = "hwy"),

      radioButtons("color", "Color points by:",
                   choices = c("Class" = "class", "Drive type" = "drv",
                               "Year" = "year", "None" = "none"),
                   selected = "class"),

      hr(),
      actionButton("reset", "Reset filters", icon = icon("rotate-left")),
      downloadButton("download", "Download data")
    ),

    mainPanel(
      textOutput("count"),
      br(),
      tabsetPanel(
        tabPanel("Plot",    plotOutput("scatter", height = "450px")),
        tabPanel("Summary", tableOutput("summary")),
        tabPanel("Data",    tableOutput("table"))
      )
    )
  )
)

# ---- Server --------------------------------------------------
server <- function(input, output, session) {

  # One reactive expression feeds every output below.
  # It re-runs only when one of the filter inputs changes.
  filtered <- reactive({
    cars |>
      filter(class %in% input$class,
             year  %in% input$year,
             displ >= input$displ[1],
             displ <= input$displ[2])
  })

  output$count <- renderText({
    paste(nrow(filtered()), "of", nrow(cars), "cars match your filters.")
  })

  output$scatter <- renderPlot({
    # validate() shows a friendly message instead of an error
    validate(need(nrow(filtered()) > 0, "No cars match these filters."))

    p <- ggplot(filtered(), aes(x = .data[[input$x]], y = .data[[input$y]]))

    if (input$color == "none") {
      p <- p + geom_point(size = 3, alpha = 0.7, color = "steelblue")
    } else {
      color_labels <- c(class = "Class", drv = "Drive type", year = "Year")
      p <- p +
        geom_point(aes(color = factor(.data[[input$color]])),
                   size = 3, alpha = 0.7) +
        labs(color = color_labels[[input$color]])
    }

    p +
      labs(x = names(num_vars)[num_vars == input$x],
           y = names(num_vars)[num_vars == input$y]) +
      theme_minimal(base_size = 15)
  })

  output$summary <- renderTable({
    filtered() |>
      group_by(class) |>
      summarise(cars         = n(),
                avg_city_mpg = mean(cty),
                avg_hwy_mpg  = mean(hwy)) |>
      arrange(desc(avg_hwy_mpg))
  }, digits = 1)

  output$table <- renderTable({
    filtered() |>
      select(manufacturer, model, year, class, displ, cyl, drv, cty, hwy)
  })

  # observeEvent() runs code for its side effect (here: changing inputs)
  observeEvent(input$reset, {
    updateSelectInput(session, "class", selected = sort(unique(cars$class)))
    updateCheckboxGroupInput(session, "year", selected = c(1999, 2008))
    updateSliderInput(session, "displ", value = range(cars$displ))
  })

  output$download <- downloadHandler(
    filename = function() "mpg-filtered.csv",
    content  = function(file) write.csv(filtered(), file, row.names = FALSE)
  )
}

shinyApp(ui, server)

title: Interactive Apps and Dashboards with Shiny
text:
Definition

A dashboard is a single screen showing the most important information about something, at a glance.


Named after a car dashboard: speed, fuel, warnings, all visible without digging
Purpose: monitoring and quick decisions
Not for: deep, step-by-step analysis or long explanations

Everyday examples

Fitness app: steps, heart rate, sleep this week
Weather app: temperature now, forecast, alerts
Course LMS: grades, upcoming deadlines, announcements

title: Interactive Apps and Dashboards with Shiny
text:
Core building blocks










Key metrics: headline numbers (total sales, average score, number of cases)
Visualizations: a few focused charts showing trends or comparisons
Filters and controls: let users focus on what matters to them
Layout: controls in a sidebar, content arranged by importance

title: Interactive Apps and Dashboards with Shiny
text:
Design principles

Know your audience: what questions do they need answered?
Most important first: people read top-left to bottom-right, so headline numbers go at the top
Less is more: every element must earn its place
Be consistent: same colors, units, and number formats everywhere
Label clearly: plain-language titles (“Bigger engines, lower mileage”) beat variable names (displ vs hwy)
Make it honest: start bar charts at zero, show units, cite the data source

title: Interactive Apps and Dashboards with Shiny
text:
Dashboard vs. report
Report

Tells one story, once
Usually static (PDF, web page, slides)
The author decides what you see
Written for reading start to finish
Example: a Quarto website or research paper

Dashboard

Answers many questions, repeatedly
Interactive and often regularly updated
The user decides what to look at
Built for scanning and exploring
Example: a live sales or public health tracker

title: Interactive Apps and Dashboards with Shiny
section: Why does a dashboard need a server?
text:
Why does a dashboard need a server?
You can already make interactive charts without Shiny (for example with Plotly or htmlwidgets). So why run R behind the page?










Client-side: interactivity with the data you already shipped
Server-side: interactivity that can do new work every time a user clicks

title: Interactive Apps and Dashboards with Shiny
text:
Reasons to use a server
Data

Live data: connect to a database or API that updates constantly; users always see the latest numbers
Big data: the server summarizes millions of rows and sends back only the result; an HTML chart would have to embed every row

Computation

Real analysis on demand: fit a model, run a simulation, or make a forecast from the user’s inputs
Generated outputs: build a custom PDF report or a filtered CSV download

Security

Privacy: raw data never leaves the server; users only see summaries
Logins: different users can see different data
Secrets: passwords and API keys stay on the server, never in the page

Two-way apps

Uploads: users analyze their own files
Writing back: forms, surveys, and annotations saved to a database

title: Interactive Apps and Dashboards with Shiny
text:
The trade-off
Client-side (Plotly, htmlwidgets)

Free and easy to host (any static site, like a Quarto website)
Works offline once loaded
Limited to the data in the page
Anyone can download that data

Server-side (Shiny)

Can do anything R can do
Data can be big, live, and private
Needs a running R server somewhere
Hosting takes setup, and may cost money at scale

Rule of thumb: if a static chart answers the question, use a static chart. Reach for Shiny when users need the app to compute something new.

title: Interactive Apps and Dashboards with Shiny
text:
What is bslib?

An R package from Posit for layouts and themes in Shiny and R Markdown / Quarto
Built on Bootstrap 5, the most popular web styling toolkit
Actively maintained; the recommended way to build Shiny dashboards today

What changes, what stays the same

Same: inputs, outputs, render*() functions, reactive(), the whole server
Different: only the UI functions that arrange things on the page


Shiny is the engine. bslib is the car body around it.

App 3: Hello, bslib!
The smallest possible dashboard: toy data, one slider, two value boxes, one chart.
# ------------------------------------------------------------
# App 3: Hello, bslib!
# The smallest possible dashboard: a sidebar, two value boxes,
# and one chart card. Uses made-up (toy) data.
#
# Same Shiny engine as App 1. Only the UI functions change:
#   fluidPage()  ->  page_sidebar()
#   panels       ->  card() and value_box()
#
# Run it:  shiny::runApp("03-hello-bslib")
# ------------------------------------------------------------

library(shiny)
library(bslib)

# Toy data: daily visitors to a coffee shop for 60 days
set.seed(42)
coffee <- data.frame(
  day      = 1:60,
  visitors = round(120 + 2 * (1:60) + rnorm(60, sd = 15))
)

# ---- UI ------------------------------------------------------
ui <- page_sidebar(
  title = "Coffee Shop Dashboard",

  sidebar = sidebar(
    sliderInput("days", "Show the last N days:",
                min = 7, max = 60, value = 30)
  ),

  # Two headline numbers side by side
  layout_columns(
    value_box(
      title = "Total visitors",
      value = textOutput("total"),
      showcase = icon("users"),
      theme = "primary"
    ),
    value_box(
      title = "Average per day",
      value = textOutput("average"),
      showcase = icon("mug-hot"),
      theme = "secondary"
    )
  ),

  # One chart in a card
  card(
    card_header("Daily visitors"),
    plotOutput("trend")
  )
)

# ---- Server --------------------------------------------------
server <- function(input, output, session) {

  recent <- reactive({
    tail(coffee, input$days)
  })

  output$total   <- renderText(format(sum(recent()$visitors), big.mark = ","))
  output$average <- renderText(round(mean(recent()$visitors)))

  output$trend <- renderPlot({
    plot(recent()$day, recent()$visitors, type = "b", pch = 19,
         col = "steelblue", xlab = "Day", ylab = "Visitors")
  })
}

shinyApp(ui, server)

text:
App 4: full code
# ------------------------------------------------------------
# App 4: Fuel Economy Dashboard (final product)
# A polished but beginner-friendly bslib dashboard built on the
# mpg dataset from ggplot2.
#
# Structure:
#   sidebar      -> filters (inputs)
#   value boxes  -> headline numbers
#   cards        -> two charts and a table
#   reactive()   -> one filtered dataset shared by every output
#
# Run it:  shiny::runApp("04-mpg-dashboard")
# ------------------------------------------------------------

library(shiny)
library(bslib)
library(ggplot2)
library(dplyr)

# ---- Data ----------------------------------------------------
cars <- mpg |>
  mutate(
    drive = recode(drv, "f" = "Front", "r" = "Rear", "4" = "4WD"),
    make  = tools::toTitleCase(manufacturer)
  )

all_classes <- sort(unique(cars$class))

# ---- Theme ---------------------------------------------------
my_theme <- bs_theme(
  version   = 5,
  bootswatch = "flatly",
  primary   = "#2C7FB8"
)

# Shared ggplot style so every chart looks consistent
theme_dash <- theme_minimal(base_size = 14) +
  theme(panel.grid.minor = element_blank(),
        legend.position  = "bottom")

# ---- UI ------------------------------------------------------
ui <- page_sidebar(
  title = "Fuel Economy Dashboard",
  theme = my_theme,

  sidebar = sidebar(
    width = 280,

    selectInput("class", "Vehicle class",
                choices  = c("All classes", all_classes),
                selected = "All classes"),

    checkboxGroupInput("year", "Model year",
                       choices  = c(1999, 2008),
                       selected = c(1999, 2008),
                       inline   = TRUE),

    checkboxGroupInput("drive", "Drive type",
                       choices  = c("Front", "Rear", "4WD"),
                       selected = c("Front", "Rear", "4WD")),

    sliderInput("cyl", "Cylinders",
                min = 4, max = 8, value = c(4, 8), step = 1),

    hr(),
    p(class = "text-muted small",
      "Data: ggplot2::mpg, EPA fuel economy for 38 popular models, 1999 and 2008.")
  ),

  # Row 1: headline numbers
  layout_columns(
    fill = FALSE,
    value_box(
      title = "Cars selected",
      value = textOutput("n_cars"),
      showcase = icon("car"),
      theme = "primary"
    ),
    value_box(
      title = "Average highway MPG",
      value = textOutput("avg_hwy"),
      showcase = icon("road"),
      theme = "success"
    ),
    value_box(
      title = "Average city MPG",
      value = textOutput("avg_cty"),
      showcase = icon("city"),
      theme = "info"
    )
  ),

  # Row 2: two charts side by side
  layout_columns(
    col_widths = c(7, 5),
    card(
      full_screen = TRUE,
      card_header("Bigger engines, lower mileage"),
      plotOutput("scatter")
    ),
    card(
      full_screen = TRUE,
      card_header("Highway MPG by manufacturer"),
      plotOutput("by_make")
    )
  ),

  # Row 3: table of the most efficient cars
  card(
    card_header("Top 10 most fuel-efficient models (highway)"),
    tableOutput("top10")
  )
)

# ---- Server --------------------------------------------------
server <- function(input, output, session) {

  # One filtered dataset, reused by every output
  filtered <- reactive({
    data <- cars |>
      filter(year  %in% input$year,
             drive %in% input$drive,
             cyl   >= input$cyl[1],
             cyl   <= input$cyl[2])

    if (input$class != "All classes") {
      data <- filter(data, class == input$class)
    }
    data
  })

  # Friendly message when the filters remove every car
  check_data <- function() {
    validate(need(nrow(filtered()) > 0,
                  "No cars match these filters. Try widening them."))
  }

  # ---- Value boxes ----
  output$n_cars  <- renderText(nrow(filtered()))
  output$avg_hwy <- renderText({
    check_data()
    round(mean(filtered()$hwy), 1)
  })
  output$avg_cty <- renderText({
    check_data()
    round(mean(filtered()$cty), 1)
  })

  # ---- Charts ----
  output$scatter <- renderPlot({
    check_data()
    ggplot(filtered(), aes(displ, hwy, color = drive)) +
      geom_jitter(size = 3, alpha = 0.7, width = 0.05, height = 0.3) +
      scale_color_manual(values = c(Front = "#2C7FB8", Rear = "#E6550D",
                                    `4WD` = "#31A354")) +
      labs(x = "Engine size (liters)", y = "Highway MPG", color = "Drive") +
      theme_dash
  })

  output$by_make <- renderPlot({
    check_data()
    filtered() |>
      group_by(make) |>
      summarise(hwy = mean(hwy)) |>
      ggplot(aes(x = hwy, y = reorder(make, hwy))) +
      geom_col(fill = "#2C7FB8") +
      geom_text(aes(label = round(hwy, 1)), hjust = -0.2, size = 4) +
      scale_x_continuous(expand = expansion(mult = c(0, 0.15))) +
      labs(x = "Average highway MPG", y = NULL) +
      theme_dash
  })

  # ---- Table ----
  output$top10 <- renderTable({
    check_data()
    filtered() |>
      arrange(desc(hwy), desc(cty)) |>
      distinct(make, model, year, .keep_all = TRUE) |>
      slice_head(n = 10) |>
      transmute(Make = make, Model = model, Year = as.integer(year),
                Class = class, Drive = drive,
                `City MPG` = as.integer(cty), `Highway MPG` = as.integer(hwy))
  }, striped = TRUE, hover = TRUE, width = "100%")
}

Close RStudio and the app is gone

Deploying = moving the app from your laptop to a server so anyone can open a link.

Workplaces

title: Interactive Apps and Dashboards with Shiny
text:
Deploying to shinyapps.io
One-time setup

Create a free account at shinyapps.io
Install the deployment package: install.packages("rsconnect")
In shinyapps.io go to Account > Tokens, click Show, and copy the command:

rsconnect::setAccountInfo(name   = "your-account",
                          token  = "XXXXXXXX",
                          secret = "XXXXXXXX")
Every deploy

RStudio: click the blue Publish button next to Run App, or
Console:

rsconnect::deployApp("apps/04-mpg-dashboard")

A few minutes later you get a link like https://your-account.shinyapps.io/04-mpg-dashboard/
The free tier limits the number of apps and active hours per month

title: Interactive Apps and Dashboards with Shiny
text:
Deployment gotchas

Use relative paths: read.csv("data/cars.csv"), never read.csv("C:/Users/me/Desktop/cars.csv")
Keep data inside the app folder: the server only receives what is in that folder
Load every package with library() at the top: this is how the server knows what to install
No install.packages() in app.R
Never put passwords in your code: use environment variables for API keys and database logins
Test locally first: if it does not run on your machine, it will not run on the server
Read the logs: a gray “Disconnected from the server” screen means an R error; the logs on shinyapps.io tell you which one

title: Interactive Apps and Dashboards with Shiny
text:
Bonus: Shinylive (no server needed)
Shinylive runs R inside the browser using WebAssembly.
install.packages("shinylive")

# convert an app folder into a static website folder
shinylive::export("apps/03-hello-bslib", "site")

# preview it locally
httpuv::runStaticServer("site")

The site/ folder can be hosted anywhere static files go (GitHub Pages, a Quarto website)
A Quarto extension (quarto-ext/shinylive) can embed apps directly in a Quarto page

But remember Part 2: everything runs on the viewer’s machine, so

All data is downloaded to the browser (nothing private)
No live database connections or server secrets
First load is slower, and not every R package is supported

title: Interactive Apps and Dashboards with Shiny
text:
Key takeaways

A Shiny app = UI + server + shinyApp(ui, server)
Inputs are read with input$id; outputs are written with output$id <- render*()
Reactivity: when an input changes, everything that uses it updates automatically
reactive() computes shared results once and reuses them
A dashboard shows the most important information at a glance
Use a server when the app must compute, protect, or fetch something new
bslib turns a Shiny app into a modern dashboard by changing only the UI
Deploy to shinyapps.io so others can use your app with just a link

activity_profile <- map_dfr(activity_columns, function(code) {
  x <- atus_full[[code]]

    code = code,
    # number of respondents with positive minutes for activity

    # Percentage of respondents with nonmissing values who recorded positive minutes
    pct_positive = round(mean(x > 0, na.rm = TRUE) * 100, 2),
    n_missing = sum(is.na(x)),
    # for respondent variables: -1 = blank, -2 = Don't know, -3 = Refused
    n_negative = sum(x < 0, na.rm = TRUE),
    n_distinct = n_distinct(x)
  )

1.3 3. Inventory and Profile Tables

1.3.1 activity_inventory
One row per activity code, containing: - code: Original ATUS activity variable name - tier_1: Broad activity category (first two digits) - tier_2: Subcategory (first four digits) - tier_3: Specific activity (all six digits)
Use: Understanding the activity classification hierarchy, and locating codes in the Activity Lexicon


1.3.2 activity_profile
One row per acticity code, containing: - code: ATUS activity variable - n_positive: Number of respondents reporting positive minutes - pct_positive: Percentage of nonissing observations reporting positive minutes - n_missing: Number of missing values - n_negative: Number of negative values (see above key) - n_distinct: Number of distinct recorded values - tier_1, tier_2, tier_3: Activity classification hierarchy
Use: Identifying common/rare activities, checking data completeness, investigating unusual values


1.3.3 resp_inventory
One row per non-activity variable, containing: - variable: Original ATUS variable name - tpye: R data class
Use: Identifying available respondent variables and checking how R imported them (some ought to be factored/otherwise altered)
Note: Some variables are numeric, but not continuous. Many characteristics are numerically coded categories.

text:
1.5 5. Important Data Considerations
Survey structure - Activity Summary contains one row per respondent - Activity variables measure minutes spent on an activity during one diary day. - Zero minutes generally means that activity wass not recorded on that day - The Activity file records individual activity episodes, not one row per respondent
Respondent coding - Many categorical variables use numeric codes - Special values may incude -1 (blank), -2 (don’t know), and -3 (refused) - Consult the corresponding data dictionary before interpreting values or replacing them with NA
Survey weighting - Current counts, distributions, and activity_profile percentages are unweighted sample descriptions - Population-level time-use estimates require appropriate AGUS survey weights - TUFNWGTP is the standard final weight for most years, but 2020 requires special treatment
2020 - ATUS collection suspended from mid-march to mid-may 2020 - Full-year estimates for 2020 are not representative - Preserve 2020 in atus_full, but use atus_complete_years when comparing complete calendar years - Special 2020 comparisons require differing weights
